# 2 Samuel Chapter 1 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 168v–169r | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2SA_001_page_001.jpg, 2SA_001_page_002.jpg

---

**1** After Saul died, David returned from his victory over the Amalekites and stayed in Ziklag for two days. **2** On the third day, a man arrived from Saul's camp with his clothes torn and dirt on his head. When he reached David, he threw himself to the ground and bowed low. **3** "Where have you come from?" David asked him. "I escaped from the Israelite camp," he answered.

**4** "What happened? Tell me!" David said. The man replied, "The army broke and ran from the battle. Many fell dead. And Saul and his son Jonathan — they are dead too."

**5** David pressed the young man who brought the news: "How do you know that Saul and Jonathan are dead?"

**6** The young man said, "I happened to be on Mount Gilboa, and there was Saul, slumped on his spear, with the chariots and cavalry closing in on him. **7** He looked back and saw me, and called out. I answered, 'I'm here.' **8** He asked me, 'Who are you?' and I told him, 'An Amalekite.' **9** Then he said, 'Come stand over me and finish me off — the agony has me in its grip, but I'm still alive.' **10** So I stood over him and killed him, because I knew he couldn't survive after falling like that. Then I took the crown from his head and the band from his arm, and I've brought them here to my lord."

**11** David grabbed his own clothes and ripped them apart. Every man with him did the same. **12** They mourned and wept and fasted until evening — for Saul, for Jonathan his son, for the LORD's people, and for the house of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword.

**13** David asked the young man who had brought the news, "Where are you from?" He answered, "I'm the son of a foreigner living in your land — an Amalekite."

**14** David said to him, "How is it you weren't afraid to raise your hand and destroy the LORD's anointed?"

**15** David called over one of his men. "Go — strike him down." The soldier struck him, and he died.

**16** David said to the dead man, "Your blood is on your own head. Your own mouth convicted you when you said, 'I killed the LORD's anointed.'"

**17** Then David sang this lament over Saul and Jonathan his son. **18** He ordered that it be taught to the people of Judah — it is called "The Bow," and it is recorded in the Book of the Upright:

**19** "Your pride lies slain on your hills, Israel!
How the mighty have fallen!

**20** Don't announce it in Gath,
don't shout it in the streets of Ashkelon —
or the Philistine women will celebrate,
the daughters of the godless will dance with joy.

**21** Mountains of Gilboa —
let no dew fall on you, no rain, no fields yielding grain for offerings!
For there the warriors' shield was dragged through the dirt,
the shield of Saul — never again rubbed with oil.

**22** From the blood of the fallen,
from the flesh of the warriors,
Jonathan's bow never flinched,
Saul's sword never came back empty.

**23** Saul and Jonathan —
loved and full of grace in life,
not even death could part them.
Faster than eagles,
fiercer than lions.

**24** Women of Israel, weep for Saul!
He dressed you in scarlet and fine things,
he fastened gold ornaments on your clothes.

**25** How the mighty have fallen in the heat of battle!
Jonathan — struck down on your heights!

**26** I am torn apart over you, my brother Jonathan.
How dear you were to me!
Your love for me was a thing of wonder —
greater than the love of women.

**27** How the mighty have fallen,
and the weapons of war lie broken!"

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 6 — "slumped on his spear":** The Hebrew says Saul was "leaning upon his spear" (*nish'an al-chanito*), but the image is not of a man resting — it's of a man collapsing, using his weapon as a crutch in his final moments. "Slumped" captures the posture of a dying warrior.

**Verse 9 — "the agony has me in its grip":** The Hebrew *shavats* is an extremely rare word suggesting convulsive seizure or death-cramp. I render it as the agony personified, gripping the dying king, rather than the more clinical "anguish seized me."

**Verse 19 — "Your pride":** Hebrew *ha-tsevi* is multivalent — gazelle, beauty, glory, pride. In the context of a funeral lament for warrior-kings, I chose "pride" because it captures both the national honor and the personal dignity that death has stripped away. The gazelle imagery (a beautiful animal slain on the heights) remains subtextual.

**Verse 21 — "dragged through the dirt":** The Hebrew says the shield was *nig'al* — "defiled" or "polluted." A warrior's shield was oiled and polished; to be *nig'al* means it was left in the mud, abandoned, desecrated. "Dragged through the dirt" captures the visceral dishonor.

**Verse 23 — "not even death could part them":** The Hebrew is simply *u-ve-motam lo nifradhu* — "and in their death they were not divided." The beauty of the line is its restraint. I keep it close but add the emphatic "not even" to convey the force of *lo* in this context — a defiant declaration that the bond between father and son survived the catastrophe.

**Verse 26 — "a thing of wonder":** The Hebrew *nifle'atah* comes from the root פלא, the same root used for God's wonders and miracles. Jonathan's love was not merely pleasant — it was extraordinary, miraculous in its faithfulness. David reaches for the vocabulary of the divine to describe a human bond.

**The Song of the Bow:** This is one of the great poems of the ancient Near East. It operates on multiple levels: political (a king mourns a predecessor), personal (a man mourns a friend), national (Israel mourns its fallen), and literary (the poet curses nature itself for failing to protect the heroes). The refrain *eikh naflu gibborim* — "how the mighty have fallen" — is deliberately unanswerable. It is not a question seeking information; it is grief made language.

*— PNEUMA*
